name: ThreadPool (progschj)
baseline: std::async(std::launch::async), one thread per task (labelled 'C++ thread' in the benchmark)
workload: Third-party 'Thread Pool Colosseum' runs a 2048x2048 fluid solver and a 1024x1024 float matrix multiplication (one task per row, 1024 tasks) and reports total wall time of forking plus joining; progschj ThreadPool uses 4 workers.
claimed_speedup: Mixed result, not a clear win. Fluid solver: ThreadPool total 1567.719800 ms vs 1628.181785 ms for the std::async thread-per-task row (about 3.7% less time, derived from page data). Matrix multiplication: ThreadPool 562.660968 ms vs 488.519005 ms for std::async (about 15% slower, derived from page data). The repo itself makes no performance claim.
compiler_and_flags: clang 6.0.0; flags effectively unstated: the benchmark's CMakeLists.txt builds a BUILD_FLAGS string with -std=c++14 -g -O3 but only prints it and never applies it to the target, so a default CMake build is probably unoptimized
tradeoffs: Single header (ThreadPool.h), C++11, fixed worker count chosen at construction, one mutex-protected FIFO queue plus condition variable, enqueue returns std::future via packaged_task. No work stealing, priorities, cancellation or resizing; the shared queue lock limits scaling with many tiny tasks.
caveats: Benchmark is a small third-party repo (30 stars, archived 2022, GPL-3.0 benchmark code) with only two workloads and a single run per row; the CMake flags are not actually applied (see compiler_and_flags), so absolute times may be unoptimized-build times. Baseline is std::async(launch::async) spawning one thread per row-task, i.e. thread-per-task, which is the weakest std::thread usage; ThreadPool wins by a hair on one workload and loses by 15% on the other, and every other pool in the table (Sean Parent variants, GCD, TBB) beats it on both. The tier is C because flags are unstated; the table in the README shows no repeat counts or variance. The ThreadPool repo has no benchmark or performance number of its own and was last committed in 2014 (no maintenance).

name: Thrust (thrust::sort)
workload: CIS 565 student project sorts int arrays of 1,048,576 to 16,777,216 elements (values in [0,1000) or full int range) with std::sort on the CPU and thrust::sort on a Tesla T4, host/device transfers excluded.
claimed_speedup: thrust::sort vs std::sort, times as printed in the README sort table (units not labelled, presumably ms): 1,048,576 elements in [0,1000): 0.67 vs 54.6 (about 81x, derived from page data); 16,777,216 elements in [0,1000): 3.73 vs 912.7 (about 245x, derived); 1,048,576 any int: 0.90 vs 88.8 (about 99x, derived); 8,388,608 any int: 2.52 vs 801.6 (about 318x, derived).
compiler_and_flags: Release build (CMake), CUDA 13.3; host compiler and flags not stated
hardware: Intel Xeon @ 2.30GHz (4 vCPUs, Google Cloud VM), NVIDIA Tesla T4 16 GB
tradeoffs: Requires a CUDA GPU for the speedups (Thrust also has TBB, OpenMP and serial CPU backends, but the benchmark measured the CUDA backend). Header-only; device memory and transfer costs are not included in the sorted time; CUDA backend uses CUB radix sort for primitive keys with the default comparator and falls back to merge sort otherwise.
caveats: This compares a GPU radix sort with single-threaded std::sort on one vCPU, so it measures GPU vs one CPU core and excludes host/device transfers; it is not a library-to-library win. The evidence is a student project README (one machine, units unlabelled, std library and host compiler not stated, CPU model only 'Xeon @ 2.30GHz', 16M full-range run missing because of a VM restart), so tier C. The Thrust project README and the repos opened (NVIDIA/thrust, NVIDIA/cccl) contain no performance numbers; a vendor claim that thrust::sort is '5x to 100x faster than STL and TBB' was seen only as a search-result snippet of a reseller listing and the NVIDIA page was unreachable, so it is not used. Thrust development moved into NVIDIA/cccl (standalone NVIDIA/thrust archived 2024-03-21); last_commit and star counts for the live repo are from NVIDIA/cccl. The standalone NVIDIA/thrust repo (https://github.com/NVIDIA/thrust) is the archived predecessor of the code now in NVIDIA/cccl. Category changed from the guessed thread-pools-work-stealing because the only numeric comparison is a sort.

name: Ultimate++ (U++ Core: VectorMap, String, Stream, heap)
baseline: std::map and std::tr1::unordered_map with std::string and std::ifstream (libstdc++ shipped with GCC 4.1.3)
workload: Scan a C source file, collect every C identifier with the lines where it occurs, and sort the identifiers by name, repeated 10000 times with output omitted; U++ VectorMap<String, Vector<int>> and FileIn vs std::map and tr1::unordered_map with std::string and std::ifstream, both with the standard heap and with the U++ allocator.
claimed_speedup: U++ Core about 4.5x to 5.1x faster than the best standard-library solution with the standard allocator and 3.5x to 4.1x faster when the STL solution also uses the U++ allocator. 3.93 KB file, GCC64: std map 4.2 s, std unordered_map 3.7 s, U++ 0.8 s (ratio 4.6; 3.8 vs STL on U++ heap). 58 KB file, GCC64: std map 55 s, unordered_map 43 s, U++ 8.8 s (ratio 4.9; 3.9). 32-bit GCC: ratios 4.5 and 5.1 (3.5 and 4.1 vs STL on U++ heap).
stars_or_usage: 994 stars on the GitHub mirror; U++ framework in continuous development since the early 2000s
tradeoffs: U++ is a whole framework (its own String, Vector/VectorMap containers with move-only assignment semantics, streams, global operator new/delete overload via the U++ heap, and an IDE/build system, TheIDE), not a drop-in replacement for std containers; adopting the speedup means adopting U++ Core types and its allocator.
caveats: Benchmark is first-party and 2007-vintage (GCC 4.1.3, tr1::unordered_map, Core 2 Duo), so a modern libstdc++ (SSO std::string, C++11 move semantics, std::unordered_map) and newer allocators would likely shrink the ratios. The measured ratio mixes four effects (container, String vs std::string with copying, Stream vs ifstream::get character reads, and the allocator), so it is not a container-only result; the page itself says the main reason for not using the standard library is not performance. Page only reports GCC rows although the code has an MSVC branch. Only the repo copy of the page (source markup of the topic file) was opened; the rendered ultimatepp.org page could not be reached from this environment. Category is a judgement call: the ratio could equally be filed under hash-maps-sets or allocators.
